Body of fundamental principles or established precedents that form the legal basis of a state, organization, or other entity and commonly determine how it is governed. A constitution written down in one or more documents is a written constitution; one contained in a single comprehensive document is codified. The [[United Kingdom]] is a notable example of an uncodified constitution, set out instead in numerous acts of a legislature, court cases, and [[Treaty|treaties]]. A treaty establishing an international organization is also its constitution.

Within states, a constitution defines the principles on which the state is based and the procedure by which laws are made, and by whom. Some constitutions, especially codified ones, also limit state power by establishing lines rulers cannot cross, such as fundamental rights. Changes frequently require consensus or a supermajority. In most modern states the constitution has supremacy over ordinary statutory law, and an official act beyond the powers it grants is null and void from inception.

The word comes through French from Latin *constitutio*, used for imperial enactments, and was later used in canon law for a decree issued by the [[Pope]]. [[William Blackstone]] used it for violations of public trust serious enough to justify a revolutionary response.

The [[Constitution of India]] is the longest written constitution of any country, with 146,385 words in English; Monaco's is the shortest, with 3,814. The constitution of [[San Marino]] might be the oldest active written one, with core documents in operation since 1600, while the [[Constitution of the United States]] is the oldest active codified one. The historical life expectancy of a written constitution since 1789 is approximately 19 years.

Process of delivering buildings, infrastructure, industrial facilities, and associated activities through to the end of their life. It typically begins with planning, financing, and design and continues until the asset is built and ready for use. It also covers repair, maintenance, expansion, and eventual demolition or decommissioning.

The industry contributes significantly to many countries' gross domestic product ([[Gross domestic product|GDP]]). Global expenditure was about $4 trillion in 2012; in 2022 it exceeded $11 trillion a year, about 13 percent of global GDP, and was forecast to reach around $14.8 trillion in 2030. Construction is also one of the most hazardous industries: about 20% (1,061) of U.S. industry fatalities in 2019 occurred in it.

The word derives from [[Latin]] *constructio*, from *com-* ("together") and *struere* ("to pile up"). The first huts and shelters were built by hand with simple tools. As cities grew during the [[Bronze Age]], professional craftsmen such as bricklayers and carpenters appeared, and in the [[Middle Ages]] artisans were organized into craft guilds. Steam-powered machinery arrived in the 19th century, followed by diesel- and electric-powered vehicles such as [[Crane (machine)|cranes]], excavators, and bulldozers.

There are three broad sectors. Building construction is divided into residential and non-residential and must conform to local codes; available materials generally dictate whether brick, stone, or timber is used. Infrastructure, or heavy civil work, includes dams, bridges, highways, railways, and water and utility systems, and overlaps with [[Civil engineering]]. Industrial construction includes offshore energy installations, [[Mining|mining]] and quarrying, refineries, chemical processing, and manufacturing plants.

Large terrestrial geographic region, identified by convention rather than strict criteria. A continent may be a single large landmass, a landmass with nearby islands, or part of a larger landmass, as Asia and Europe are within [[Eurasia]]. The number recognized varies from seven to as few as four. Most English-speaking countries recognize seven; in order of area, they are Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, and Australia (or Oceania or Australasia). Variants merge regions, for example North and South America into the [[Americas]].

The criterion "large" is arbitrary: Greenland, at 2,166,086 sq km, is classed as the largest island, while Australia, at 7,617,930 sq km, is deemed the smallest continent. Most Pacific island countries and territories are grouped with Australia as Oceania.

In geology, a continent is "one of Earth's major landmasses, including both dry land and continental shelves." Geological continents correspond to seven large areas of continental crust on the tectonic plates and exclude small fragments such as [[Madagascar]], called microcontinents. Four criteria apply: high elevation relative to the ocean floor; a wide range of silica-rich rocks; crust thicker than the surrounding oceanic crust; and well-defined limits around a large enough area. Continental crust is known only on Earth, and emerged continental land covers approximately 29% of its surface. Debate continues over the submerged [[Zealandia]].

The English word dates from the 16th century, from Latin *terra continens*, "continuous land," and was once applied to small areas. Continental drift, which gained recognition in the 20th century, holds that the present continents formed from the breakup of the supercontinent [[Pangaea]] hundreds of millions of years ago.

Art, science, and craft of using heat to make food more palatable, digestible, nutritious, or safe. Also called cookery, it ranges from grilling over an open [[Fire|fire]] to ovens and boiling, reflecting local conditions and traditions. It is an aspect of all human societies and a cultural universal. Preparing food with heat is an activity unique to humans.

Archaeological evidence of cooking fires dates to at least 300,000 years ago, though some estimate that humans began cooking as early as 2 million years ago. Controlled fire at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa dates to 1 million years ago, and the oldest evidence of cooking, heated fish teeth from a deep cave, dates to about 780,000 years ago. Richard Wrangham suggested that early [[Homo habilis]] cooked regularly, but unequivocal evidence for controlled fire begins at 400,000 BCE. Widespread cooking fires are thought to have begun about 250,000 years ago, when hearths first appeared.

Techniques include dry-heat methods such as grilling and frying, moist-heat methods such as steaming and simmering, and combination methods such as braising. Cooking manipulates the chemistry of the proteins, carbohydrates, and fats in ingredients; heating sugars with proteins causes the [[Maillard reaction]], a basic flavor-enhancing process.

The invention of [[Pottery|pottery]] for boiling water expanded techniques. The [[Columbian exchange]] transformed cuisines: [[Potato|potatoes]], tomatoes, maize, chocolate, and vanilla reached the Old World, while cattle, wheat, rice, and apples reached the New. In the 19th century, cuisine became a symbol of national identity. The [[Industrial Revolution]] brought mass production, canning, and standardization of food, and fast food restaurants emerged in the 1920s.

Soft, malleable, ductile metallic element (symbol Cu, from [[Latin]] *cuprum*; atomic number 29). Pure copper is orange-red, one of few metals with a natural color other than gray or silver. Its electrical conductivity is very high (59.6×10⁶ S/m), and its thermal conductivity is second only to silver among pure metals. It is used as a conductor, as a building material, and in alloys such as sterling silver, cupronickel (marine hardware and coins), and constantan (thermocouples). Electrical applications account for over 60% of consumption.

Copper is one of the few native metals, occurring naturally in usable form, which led to human use from c. 8000 BC. It was the first metal to be [[Smelting|smelted]] from sulfide ores (c. 5000 BC), the first cast in a mold (c. 4000 BC), and the first purposely alloyed with tin to make [[Bronze|bronze]] (c. 3500 BC). The name derives from Latin *aes cyprium*, "metal of [[Cyprus]]."

Copper does not react with water but slowly forms a brown-black oxide layer that, unlike rust on iron, protects the metal from further corrosion. Green verdigris forms on old copper roofs and on the [[Statue of Liberty]]. Copper(II) salts give blue or green colors to minerals such as azurite, [[Malachite|malachite]], and turquoise and have been used as pigments. Copper compounds also serve as fungicides and wood preservatives.

There are 29 isotopes; ⁶³Cu and ⁶⁵Cu are stable. Copper makes up about 50 ppm of Earth's crust, the 26th most abundant element. The largest mass of elemental copper found weighed 420 tonnes, discovered in 1857 on the Keweenaw Peninsula in [[Michigan]]. Copper is essential to all aerobic organisms; adult humans contain 1.4 to 2.1 mg per kilogram of body weight.

Legal entity authorized by the state to act as a single entity and recognized in law as a legal person. Early corporations were established by charter, an act of a monarch or legislature; most jurisdictions now allow incorporation through registration. Corporations are usually divided by whether they can issue stock and whether they are formed to make a profit.

Shareholders own a registered corporation, and their liability is generally limited to their investment. Limited liability separates control from ownership: a passive shareholder is not personally liable for the corporation's contractual obligations or torts. Supporters credit it with encouraging investment and risk-taking, while critics argue that it can encourage moral hazard.

The word derives from Latin *corpus*, "body." Roman law recognized corporate entities as *universitas*, *corpus*, or *collegium*. After the Lex Julia under [[Julius Caesar]], *collegia* required the approval of the Senate or emperor; they could own property, make contracts, and sue and be sued. The concept was revived in the 11th–14th centuries with the recovery of Justinian's [[Corpus Juris Civilis]]. Early entities carrying on business included the *sreni* of the [[Maurya Empire]] in India. The alleged oldest commercial corporation, the Stora Kopparberg mining community in Falun, [[Sweden]], received a charter in 1347.

In the 17th century, chartered companies such as the [[Dutch East India Company]] and the [[Hudson's Bay Company]] led European colonial ventures. The Dutch company defeated Portuguese forces in the Moluccas to profit from European demand for [[Spice|spices]]; its investors held paper share certificates, traded them on the Amsterdam [[Stock|stock]] exchange, and were granted limited liability. Speculation in joint-stock companies also contributed to the 1720 South Sea Bubble.

Soft, fluffy staple fiber that grows in a protective boll around the seeds of plants of the genus *Gossypium*, in the mallow family [[Malvaceae]]. The fiber is almost pure [[Cellulose|cellulose]]. The plant is a shrub native to tropical and subtropical regions of the Americas, Africa, and India; wild species are most diverse in Mexico. Cotton was domesticated independently in the Old and New Worlds. Spun into yarn or thread, it makes soft, breathable, durable cloth and is the most widely used natural fiber in clothing.

Four species are grown commercially: *Gossypium hirsutum* (upland cotton, 90% of world production), *G. barbadense* (extra-long staple, over 5%), *G. arboreum* (tree cotton, less than 2%), and *G. herbaceum* (Levant cotton, less than 2%).

The word derives ultimately from Hebrew *kuttōnĕṯ* and was the usual medieval Arabic word for cotton. [[Marco Polo]] described cotton grown in abundance in Khotan, today's Xinjiang.

Early evidence includes *G. barbadense* at Nanchoc, [[Peru]], dated to the 7th–6th millennia BC, and a cotton thread joining eight copper beads at Mehrgarh, Pakistan, dated to the sixth millennium BC. Fragments from the Bronze Age [[Indus Valley Civilisation]] date to the 3rd millennium BCE. In Mexico, *G. hirsutum* was domesticated between around 3400 and 2300 BC, and cotton sent to Aztec rulers as tribute amounted to about 53,000 tonnes annually.

The [[Cotton gin]], invented in 1793, lowered production costs, and cotton supplied the textile mills of the [[Industrial Revolution]]. World production is about 25 million tonnes, or 110 million bales, annually, on 2.5% of the world's arable land. India is the largest producer, and the United States has been the largest exporter for many years.

Political entity or its territory, a term applied to sovereign states, unrecognized states, constituent countries, and dependent territories. A country may consist of multiple nations, a structure called a multinational state. There is no universal agreement on the number of countries, because some entities are not recognized as sovereign by the UN system but are recognized by at least one member. *The Economist* wrote in 2010 that "any attempt to find a clear definition of a country soon runs into a thicket of exceptions and anomalies."

A [[Sovereign state|sovereign state]] holds supreme legitimate authority over a part of the world. The 1933 Montevideo Convention names four criteria for statehood: a permanent population, a defined territory, an effective government, and the capacity to enter relations with other states. Theorists differ on whether statehood rests on empirical existence alone or also requires recognition by others. The [[United Nations]] has 193 member states. [[Taiwan]] and [[Kosovo]] have limited recognition or actively disputed sovereignty, and breakaway states such as [[Transnistria]] have none.

Some sovereign states are unions of polities, each also called a country. The [[Danish Realm]] consists of Denmark proper, the Faroe Islands, and Greenland; the [[Kingdom of the Netherlands]] of the Netherlands proper, Aruba, Curaçao, and Sint Maarten; and the [[United Kingdom]] of England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.

The word has other senses: a rural area ("the country"), a region such as the West Country in England, native sovereign territory such as Indian country in the United States, or a qualifier, as in country music. Anthropologist Clifford Geertz wrote in 1997 that the relationships between "country" and "nation" differ too much from place to place to be reduced to a simple opposition.

Unlawful act punishable by a state or other authority. The term has no simple, universally accepted definition in modern criminal law. The most popular view is that crime is a category created by law: something is a crime if the applicable law declares it so. One proposed definition is that a crime is an act harmful not only to an individual but also to a community, society, or the state, a "public wrong."

Prohibitions on acts such as [[Murder|murder]], rape, and theft exist worldwide, but what counts as an offense is defined by the [[Criminal law|criminal law]] of each jurisdiction. In some [[Common law|common law]] nations no comprehensive criminal code exists, and courts have developed offenses themselves. Usually a crime requires both the act (*actus reus*) and criminal intent (*mens rea*), though strict liability crimes require no proof of intent. Not every violation of law is a crime: breaches of private law, such as [[Tort|torts]] and breaches of contract, are enforced through civil procedure.

Historically, criminal codes often divided offenders by class or caste, and in some tribal societies an entire clan was liable for a crime, leading to feuds lasting generations. Sentences range from community sentences to imprisonment, [[Life imprisonment|life imprisonment]], or in some jurisdictions death. Criminalization raises [[Human rights|human rights]] questions, since it can infringe on autonomy and subject people to unjust punishment.

International criminal law addresses serious offenses such as [[Genocide|genocide]], crimes against humanity, and [[War crime|war crimes]], defined through treaties and international custom. Intentional homicide rates range from under 1 per 100,000 population in many Asian and European countries to over 40 in certain Latin American and African nations. Some criminologists emphasize individual choices weighed against risks and rewards; others stress social and environmental influences.

Series of military campaigns launched by the papacy between 1095 and 1291 against Muslim rulers for the recovery and defence of the Holy Land. [[Pope Urban II]] proclaimed the [[First Crusade]] at the Council of Clermont in November 1095, calling Christians to reconquer Jerusalem with promises of spiritual reward. Its success, including the capture of Jerusalem in 1099, led to four [[Crusader states]] in the Levant: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Principality of Antioch, and the counties of Tripoli and Edessa. Large campaigns required crusade indulgences, military orders, and taxation of clerical income.

The fall of Edessa prompted the Second Crusade, which failed in 1148. [[Saladin]], having united Egypt and Muslim Syria, destroyed the Crusader armies at the Battle of Hattin in 1187. The [[Third Crusade|Third Crusade]] preserved the Crusader states, but Jerusalem remained under Muslim control. The Fourth Crusade was diverted to the Byzantine Empire, culminating in the sack of [[Constantinople]] and the establishment of the Latin Empire in 1204. Jerusalem was regained by negotiation in 1229 during the Sixth Crusade. [[Louis IX of France]] led the Seventh Crusade against Egypt (1248–51) and the Eighth against Tunis (1270); both failed. The [[Mamluk|Mamluks]] captured the last mainland strongholds in 1291.

The crusading movement expanded to campaigns against pagans, Christian dissidents, and other enemies of the papacy, including the Iberian, Albigensian, and Northern Crusades, continuing into the 18th century. Violence on both sides marked the period, including the killing of Jerusalem's inhabitants in 1099 and Saladin's executions of captives. The movement left the military orders of the Templars and Hospitallers and increased East-West exchange of goods and knowledge.
